reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods (2018)

sections.title: Axial Load Transfer
sections.body: Drilled shafts transmit axial compression and uplift loads through side resistance Rs and base (tip) resistance RB. Load transfer mechanics (Kulhawy 1991, O'Neill and Reese 1972): Side resistance mobilized first at small displacements (~1/2 inch for full mobilization); base resistance mobilizes at larger displacements (~4-5% of diameter B for cohesive soil and rock; ~10% B for cohesionless soils). Three components: side resistance Rs, base resistance RB, and combined total resistance QT. Between peak side and peak base resistance, side resistance may increase or decrease depending on stress-strain behavior at shaft-soil interface (softening possible in some materials). Design for service limit states must account for differences in mobilization displacement for side vs. base resistance.
key_points: Side resistance mobilizes at ~1/2 inch displacement; base resistance at ~4-10% of shaft diameter
Displacement for maximum base resistance: 4-5% B (cohesive/rock) or 10% B (cohesionless)
Side resistance mobilizes first; peak side and peak base occur at different displacements
Service limit state design must account for differences in side vs. base mobilization
figures: Figure 10-1: Generalized load transfer behavior of drilled shaft in compression
sections.applicability: Axial design of all drilled shafts; basis for step-by-step design procedure

sections.title: Relationship to Overall Design Process
sections.body: Chapter constitutes detailed treatment of Block 11 ('Establish Minimum Depth and Diameter for Axial Loads') of the overall design process (Figure 8-1, Chapter 8). AASHTO (2017a) identifies axial compression and uplift of single drilled shafts as strength limit states; settlement control as service limit state. Factored axial force effects communicated by structural engineer to foundation designer for each applicable limit state and scour condition. For cohesive soils in Service I load combination, transient loads can be omitted from settlement analysis.
key_points: Block 11 of overall design process: minimum depth and diameter for axial loads
Strength limit states: axial compression and uplift
Service limit state: settlement control
Transient loads may be omitted from settlement analysis in cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Relates axial design to overall design process; limit state identification

sections.title: Step-by-Step Procedure: Design for Axial Load
sections.body: 7-step LRFD design procedure: (1) Idealize subsurface profile — divide into geomaterial layers; classify each as cohesionless (GW, GP, GM, SW, SP, SM, ML), cohesive (GC, SC, CL, CH, MH), or rock. Scour conditions must be reflected in profiles. (2) Establish limit states and factored axial loads — review applicable limit states and load combinations per Chapter 8. (3) Assign geomaterial properties — cohesionless soils: SPT N60 and (N1)60, effective stress friction angle φ', σ'v; cohesive soils: undrained shear strength su; rock: uniaxial compressive strength qu, RQD, GSI. Use mean values for LRFD; COV limits: N-values ≤45%, su ≤35%. (4) Select trial lengths and diameters — L/B typically 3-30; soil depths to 100 ft and diameters to 8 ft are routine; depths to 200 ft and diameters to 12 ft are within range of well-equipped specialty contractors; rock sockets up to 50 ft possible; in-soil overburden diameter ≥6 in. larger than rock socket to allow rock drilling tools to pass. (5) Compute nominal unit side and base resistances (Step 5 — detailed design methods per Section 10.3.5). (6) Satisfy strength limit states — check ΣηiγiFi ≤ ΣφiRi; resistance factors φ per AASHTO and agency experience; iterate on length and diameter as needed. (7) Satisfy service limit states — conduct load-deformation analysis; mobilized side and base resistance at axial displacement corresponding to tolerable deformation.
key_points: 7-step procedure matching Block 11 of overall design process
Geomaterial classification: cohesionless, cohesive, or rock for each layer
Routine: soil to 100 ft depth, diameter to 8 ft; specialty: to 200 ft, to 12 ft diameter
In-soil overburden diameter ≥6 in. larger than rock socket for tool passage
COV limits: N-values ≤45%; su ≤35% for applying tabulated resistance factors
LRFD: ΣηiγiFi ≤ ΣφiRi for each applicable strength limit state

sections.title: Calculate Nominal Side and Base Resistances (Step 5)
sections.body: [p. 10-9] This step calculates the geotechnical resistances for axial compression or uplift loads. The methods are those of Article 10.8 of the 2017 AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, unless research supported by full-scale axial load tests warrants a different approach. For the two components of compression resistance (side and base), the summation of factored resistances on the right side of Equation 10-1 is: Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum over i = 1 to n of phi_S,i R_SN,i + phi_B R_BN (Eq. 10-2), where R_SN,i is the nominal side resistance of layer i, phi_S,i the resistance factor for side resistance in layer i, n the number of layers providing side resistance, R_BN the nominal base resistance and phi_B the resistance factor for base resistance. Nominal side resistance of a layer is the nominal unit side resistance f_SN times the cylindrical area, layer thickness Delta z_i times the circumference: R_SN = pi B Delta z_i f_SN (Eq. 10-3), with B the shaft diameter. Nominal base resistance is the nominal unit base resistance q_BN times the area at the base: R_BN = (pi B^2 / 4) q_BN (Eq. 10-4). Nominal unit side resistance is evaluated in effective stress for cohesionless soil layers; in total stress for end-of-construction (undrained) conditions in cohesive soil layers (effective stress analysis if the long-term, fully drained side resistance is important); and in terms of uniaxial compressive strength in rock. The methods for each category of geomaterial follow in 10.3.5.1 (cohesionless soils), 10.3.5.2 (cohesive soils) and 10.3.5.3 (rock).
key_points: Eq. 10-2: sum of factored resistances = sum of phi_S,i R_SN,i over the n side layers + phi_B R_BN
Eq. 10-3: R_SN = pi B (Delta z_i) f_SN; Eq. 10-4: R_BN = (pi B^2/4) q_BN
Side resistance: effective stress in cohesionless soil, total stress (undrained, end of construction) in cohesive soil, uniaxial compressive strength in rock
Methods follow Article 10.8 of the 2017 AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications
equations: Eq. 10-2: Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum[i=1..n](phi_S,i R_SN,i) + phi_B R_BN — factored axial compression resistance
Eq. 10-3: R_SN = pi B (Delta z_i) f_SN — nominal side resistance of layer i
Eq. 10-4: R_BN = (pi B^2 / 4) q_BN — nominal base resistance
sections.applicability: Nominal side and base resistance of drilled shafts in compression or uplift; the geomaterial-specific methods are in 10.3.5.1 to 10.3.5.3

sections.title: Cohesionless Soils
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [p. 10-10]. Nominal side resistance is the frictional resistance over the cylindrical soil-shaft interface; the unit side resistance is proportional to the normal stress on the interface (Figure 10-4). By Equation 10-3: R_SN = pi B Delta z f_SN = pi B Delta z (sigma'_v K tan delta) (Eq. 10-5), where sigma'_v is the average vertical effective stress over Delta z, K = sigma'_h/sigma'_v is the coefficient of horizontal soil stress, sigma'_h the horizontal effective stress, and delta the effective stress angle of friction for the soil-shaft interface. Combining terms: beta = K tan delta (Eq. 10-6) and f_SN = sigma'_v beta (Eq. 10-7); beta is the side resistance coefficient (the 'beta method'). Chen and Kulhawy (2002) evaluate K and delta separately and then combine them to beta. [p. 10-11] K is a function of the at-rest value K_o and of the change in horizontal stress caused by construction, K/K_o. A first-order approximation is K/K_o = 1 (no stress change from construction). For 'normal' (uncemented) soils K_o follows Mayne and Kulhawy (1982): K_o = (1 - sin phi') OCR^(sin phi') <= K_p (Eq. 10-8), with OCR = sigma'_p / sigma'_v (Eq. 10-9), sigma'_p the effective vertical preconsolidation stress, and K_p = tan^2(45 deg + phi'/2) (Eq. 10-10) the upper bound. From SPT N-values, Mayne (2007): sigma'_p / p_a ~ 0.47 (N60)^m (Eq. 10-11), with m = 0.6 for clean quartzitic sands and m = 0.8 for silty sands to sandy silts (e.g., Piedmont residual soils), p_a atmospheric pressure in the units of sigma'_p (e.g., 2,116 psf). For gravelly soils, Kulhawy and Chen (2007): sigma'_p / p_a = 0.15 N60 (Eq. 10-12). Substituting Eqs. 10-9 to 10-12 into Eq. 10-6 gives beta ~ (1 - sin phi') (sigma'_p / sigma'_v)^(sin phi') tan phi' <= K_p tan phi' (Eq. 10-13), with sigma'_p from Eq. 10-11 for sandy soils and Eq. 10-12 for gravelly soils. [pp. 10-11, 10-12] beta at shallow depth is limited to its value at a depth of 7.5 ft, a vertical effective stress of about 900 psf; at lower confining stress the correlations for friction angle and preconsolidation stress are not validated. beta from Eq. 10-13 goes into Eq. 10-7 for the unit side resistance and into Eq. 10-5 for R_SN of each cohesionless layer. The principal limitation is the reliance on N-values and their correlations with friction angle and preconsolidation stress. Resistance factors have not been established for this method by a probability-based calibration with the AASHTO LRFD load factors; calibration to ASD with a factor of safety FS = 2.5 gives phi_S = 0.55 for side resistance in cohesionless soils, recommended until a reliability-based calibration is done. The method assumes no change in K from construction, which holds for dry, slurry (wet-hole) and casing methods with minimal sidewall disturbance, proper handling of slurry and casing and prompt concrete placement; otherwise K can fall to 2/3 of K_o, or lower if the soil caves. Where permanent casing extends through cohesionless soil, AASHTO (2007a) states no specific data are available but casing reduction factors of 0.60 to 0.75 are commonly used; side resistance may be neglected over the depth of permanent casing in very soft soils or where scour is expected. Scour: all material above the total scour line is assumed removed, and the change in stress affects beta (Section 10.5). ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE 10-1 [pp. 10-12 to 10-14]: shaft B = 5 ft; layer 1 (0 to 15 ft, N60 = 9, (N1)60 = 14, gamma = 115 pcf) and layer 2 (15 to 33 ft, N60 = 27, (N1)60 = 28, gamma_sat = 125 pcf) of silty sand. The friction angle is taken as phi' = delta = 27.5 + 9.2 log[(N1)60] = 38 deg and 41 deg (Chen and Kulhawy, 2002), so delta = phi'. sigma'_v at mid-layer 862.5 and 2,288.4 psf; sigma'_p = 2,116 x 0.47 (N60)^0.8 = 5,768 and 13,890 psf; OCR 6.7 and 6.1; K_o 1.24 and 1.13 (K_p 4.20 and 4.81); beta = K tan delta = 0.97 and 0.98; f_SN = 837 and 2,248 psf (the printed layer 2 line shows beta as 1.08 while the printed summary table gives 0.98); R_SN,1 = 197.2 kips, R_SN,2 = 635.6 kips, sum 833 kips. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-14, 10-15]. Base resistance develops with downward displacement, and the displacement for full mobilization varies widely because excavation releases stress beneath the base and base cleaning varies; direct empirical correlation with SPT N-values from load tests is recommended for routine design (Reese and O'Neill, 1989): q_BN (tsf) = 0.60 N60 <= 30 tsf (Eq. 10-14), N60 the average between the base and two diameters below it, the field value with no overburden correction (at 60 percent hammer efficiency). It rests on compression tests on shafts with clean bases at settlements of five percent of the base diameter; the 30 tsf limit is the largest value in those tests. It applies to cohesionless soils with N-values of 50 blows per foot or less; above 50, load testing is recommended, otherwise q_BN is limited to the upper bound of Eq. 10-14. The resistance factor phi = 0.50 specified in AASHTO (2007) was set by fitting to FS = 2.75 with the reliability-based factors of Paikowsky et al. (2004) (Allen, 2005). Bearing capacity theory may be used instead, but because the displacement to mobilize full base resistance varies widely, Eq. 10-14 is recommended for routine design.

sections.title: Cohesive Soils
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-15 to 10-18]. Short-term undrained side resistance in cohesive layers is in terms of undrained shear strength: R_SN = pi B Delta z f_SN = pi B Delta z (alpha s_u) (Eq. 10-15), s_u the average undrained shear strength over Delta z and alpha the adhesion coefficient (the 'alpha method'). Laboratory strength tests of undisturbed samples are recommended for s_u; in-situ tests should be calibrated against laboratory tests. UC and UU tests are less reliable than CIUC triaxial tests (sample disturbance, strain rate, drainage), so UC and UU values are first converted to CIUC (Chen and Kulhawy, 1993): s_u(UC)/s_u(CIUC) = 0.893 + 0.513 log(s_u(UC)/sigma'_vo) (Eq. 10-16); s_u(UU)/s_u(CIUC) = 0.911 + 0.499 log(s_u(UU)/sigma'_vo) (Eq. 10-17), sigma'_vo the vertical effective stress. The adhesion factor (Chen et al., 2011; Figure 10-6), recommended as a revision to the expressions in AASHTO LRFD (2017a), is alpha = 0.30 + 0.17 / (s_u(CIUC)/p_a) (Eq. 10-18), p_a atmospheric pressure in consistent units. It is common practice to neglect side resistance over the top 5 ft of the shaft, or to the depth of seasonal moisture change, subject to local experience. Permanent casing through cohesive soil reduces side resistance; reduction factors of 50 to 75 percent for steel piles compared with driven concrete piles are a guide, with no specific data for cased shafts, which may sit near the lower end. Illustrative Example 10-2 [p. 10-18]: a stiff clay layer of 27 ft with mean s_u = 2,000 psf (UU): sigma'_vo = 3,697 psf, s_u/sigma'_vo = 0.541, s_u(CIUC) = 2,000 / (0.911 + 0.499 log 0.541) = 2,571 psf (as printed), alpha = 0.30 + 0.17/(2,571/2,116) = 0.44, f_SN = 1,131 psf, R_SN,3 = 479.7 kips. The alpha method assumes design for short-term undrained loading by total stress is adequate for routine design; for very heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8) the fully drained side resistance may be considered, using Eq. 10-5 with c' = 0, phi' from CD or CU triaxial tests, the interface friction angle taken equal to phi', and K = K_o from in-situ measurements or OCR. No resistance factor is recommended for fully drained side resistance in cohesive soils. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-19, 10-20]. Total stress bearing capacity (O'Neill and Reese, 1999): q_BN = N*_c s_u (Eq. 10-19), s_u the mean undrained shear strength over a depth of 2B below the base. For depth at least 3 times the diameter and s_u at least 2,000 psf, N*_c = 9.0; for smaller s_u, N*_c is taken from Table 10-2 (500 psf: 6.5; 1,000 psf: 8.0; 2,000 psf and above: 9.0; linear interpolation between). For embedment D < 3B: q_BN = (2/3) [1 + D/(6B)] N*_c s_u (Eq. 10-20), N*_c from Table 10-2. The resistance factor phi = 0.40 (Table 8-4) for base resistance by this method is based on Allen (2005), fitting to ASD FS = 2.75 and the reliability analysis of Paikowsky et al. (2004). Fully drained base resistance in heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8) can be analysed by bearing capacity theory with c' and phi'; it is not addressed in AASHTO (2017a). Example 10-3 [p. 10-20]: q_BN = 9.0 (2,571 psf) = 23.1 ksf, R_BN = pi/4 (5 ft)^2 x 23.1 ksf = 453.6 kips.

sections.title: Rock
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-20 to 10-22]. Unit side resistance in rock is evaluated from the mean uniaxial compressive strength q_u of the rock layer: f_SN / p_a = C sqrt(q_u / p_a) (Eq. 10-21), p_a atmospheric pressure in the units of q_u and C a regression coefficient from load test results. Kulhawy et al. (2005), the most recent regression of load test data, give a mean C = 1.0; Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0 is recommended for 'normal' rock sockets. q_u should come from laboratory uniaxial compression tests (ASTM) on specimens at field moisture content; estimating q_u from point load or Schmidt hammer tests may be inappropriate, and specimens allowed to dry give higher q_u and overestimate resistance. The q_u used in Eq. 10-21 should not exceed the compressive strength of the shaft concrete, unless load tests demonstrate higher side resistance. 'Normal' means sockets constructed with conventional equipment with nominally clean sidewalls and no special procedures or artificial roughening; rock prone to smearing or rapid deterioration (clay shales; Appendix B) is outside the normal range. Rock mass that cannot be excavated without caving is also outside the normal category and may show lower side resistance than Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0. Where caving or instability of the socket is anticipated (e.g., 'plug-ahead' or 'grout-ahead' installation), O'Neill and Reese (1999) is recommended: f_SN / p_a = 0.65 alpha_E sqrt(q_u / p_a) (Eq. 10-22), with alpha_E from the RQD and the joint condition in Table 10-3. Table 10-3, side resistance reduction factor for caving rock, joint modification factor alpha_E [p. 10-21]: RQD 100 percent: 1.00 (closed joints), 0.85 (open or gouge-filled joints); RQD 70: 0.85, 0.55; RQD 50: 0.60, 0.55; RQD 30: 0.50, 0.50; RQD 20: 0.45, 0.45. In summary, Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0 is recommended for routine design of rock sockets; for highly fractured or weathered rock that cannot be drilled without artificial support (casing or the plug-ahead method), or where caving is anticipated, Eq. 10-22 with the Table 10-3 reduction factors is recommended. The resistance factor recommended with Eqs. 10-21 and 10-22 is phi = 0.55, based on fitting to ASD with FS = 2.5, 'as presented in Table 8-4' (p. 10-21; Table 8-4 on p. 8-14 prints 0.50 for side resistance in rock: both are printed and are not reconciled here). [pp. 10-21, 10-22] Artificial roughening of sockets (grooving tools or other measures) can increase side resistance; regression of load test data by Kulhawy and Prakoso (2007) suggests a mean value C = 1.9 with use of Eq. 10-22 for roughened sockets. It is strongly recommended that load tests or local experience be used to verify values of C greater than 1.0. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-22 to 10-25]. q_BN = N*_cr q_u (Eq. 10-23), N*_cr an empirical bearing capacity factor for rock. Prakoso and Kulhawy (2002; Figure 10-7): 14 load tests at 9 sites, mean N*_cr = 3.38, COV = 35.4 percent; a lower bound N*_cr = 2.5 (consistent with Rowe and Armitage, 1987) incorporates most points; the Zhang and Einstein (1998) data give a mean 3.56, COV = 61.0 percent. N*_cr = 2.5 is recommended when q_u is the only parameter used and (1) the base bears on massive or tightly jointed rock (no compressible seams or joints) to at least one diameter below the base, (2) no solution cavities or voids exist beneath the base, and (3) a clean base can be achieved and verified. The AASHTO (2017a) resistance factor for Eq. 10-23 with N*_cr = 2.5 is phi = 0.50 (FS = 2.5); larger N*_cr is justified when verified by local experience or load testing. For fractured rock mass, bearing capacity with the Hoek-Brown criterion (Turner and Ramey, 2010): sigma'_1 = sigma'_3 + q_u [m_b (sigma'_3/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-24); with GSI, m_b/m_i = exp[(GSI - 100)/28] (Eq. 10-25), s = exp[(GSI - 100)/9] (Eq. 10-26), a = 1/2 + (1/6)[exp(-GSI/15) - exp(-20/3)] (Eq. 10-27). The overburden parameter A = sigma'_vb + q_u [m_b (sigma'_vb/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-28), sigma'_vb the vertical effective stress at the socket tip; q_BN = A + q_u [m_b (A/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-29). N*_cr = 2.5 can be used as an upper bound on base resistance unless local experience or load tests validate higher values (Figure 10-8). The recommended resistance factor for Eq. 10-29 is phi = 0.50 (FS = 2.5). [p. 10-25] Base resistance may instead be governed by the structural strength of the concrete in bearing (Chapter 12); the structural bearing resistance factor is phi = 0.70 against the geotechnical phi = 0.50, so the factored resistances are compared case by case. Example 10-4 [pp. 10-26 to 10-28]: 6 ft socket, 10 ft deep, q_u = 2,500 psi (360 ksf): f_SN = 2.116 x 1.0 x sqrt(300/2.116) = 27.6 ksf as printed (the printed expression evaluates to 25.2 ksf; the printed R_SN follows the 27.6), R_SN = 27.6 x (6 pi) x 10 = 5,202 kips; q_BN = 2.5 (360) = 900 ksf, R_BN = 25,447 kips, phi R_BN = 0.50 (25,447) = 12,723 kips, governing over the structural 19,380 kips.

sections.title: Evaluate Trial Design for Strength Limit States (Step 6)
sections.body: [pp. 10-28, 10-29] Step 6 applies resistance factors to the nominal resistances of Step 5 and checks each strength limit state from Step 2, for each loading mode and each trial design, against Eq. 10-1: Sum(eta_i gamma_i F_i) <= Sum(phi_i R_i). Recommended resistance factors for the nominal resistances calculated by the methods above are in Table 8-4. When compressive resistances are determined from one or more static load tests, AASHTO (2017a) allows a resistance factor as high as 0.70; the value selected is a matter of engineering judgment and accounts for the number of load tests and the subsurface variability (Chapter 13). Illustrative Example 10-5 [p. 10-29]: factored demand Sum(gamma Q) = 766 kips (Strength I). Factors from Table 8-4 as used in the example: side resistance in compression, cohesionless soil 0.55; cohesive soil 0.45; base resistance, cohesive soil 0.40. Factored resistances: layer 1 197.2 x 0.55 = 108.5 kips; layer 2 635.6 x 0.55 = 349.6 kips; layer 3 side 479.7 x 0.45 = 215.9 kips; layer 3 base 453.6 x 0.40 = 181.4 kips; Sum(phi R) = 855.4 kips. 766 kips < 855.4 kips; C/D = 855.4/766 = 1.12 > 1.0, so the trial design satisfies the strength limit state.
key_points: Eq. 10-1 check: Sum(eta gamma F) <= Sum(phi R); resistance factors from Table 8-4
Static load test: AASHTO (2017a) allows phi up to 0.70, by judgment
Example 10-5 factors: 0.55 cohesionless side, 0.45 cohesive side, 0.40 cohesive base; factored resistance 855.4 kips vs demand 766 kips
equations: Eq. 10-1: Sum(eta_i gamma_i F_i) <= Sum(phi_i R_i) — LRFD check for strength limit states

sections.title: Design for Uplift
sections.body: [pp. 10-37 to 10-40] Uplift arises, for example, where moment on a pier footing is resisted by a couple of uplift in shafts on one side and compression in shafts on the other (Figure 10-14), and from construction loads, adjacent-span loading, seismic and impact events. A shaft in uplift is resisted by its weight and by side resistance on the shaft-geomaterial interface (Figure 10-15). AASHTO (2017a) requires uplift resistance of a single straight-sided shaft to be estimated in a manner similar to side resistance in compression, so nominal unit side resistances come from the methods of Section 10.3.5. Base resistance (tip suction) is not relied on: its prediction is not sufficiently reliable. The shaft weight is treated as a negative force effect on the left side of Eq. 10-1, not as resistance, so the strength limit state is Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum over i = 1 to n of phi_S,i R_SN,i (numbered 10-32 in the print, p. 10-39). Resistance factors for uplift side resistance are in Table 8-4; the uplift values are less by 0.10 than the equivalent compression factors (Allen, 2005; AASHTO, 2017a), an interim procedure pending reliability-based calibration. Where side resistance comes from one or more static uplift load tests at the site, AASHTO (2017a) allows phi = 0.60 for all geomaterials, applied with judgment on how well production shafts match the test conditions; otherwise a lower factor is used. If the uplift is caused by an extreme event (earthquake, ice, vessel impact), the uplift resistance factor can be taken as 0.80 (p. 10-40).
key_points: Uplift resistance is side resistance only; base resistance is not relied on
Uplift phi values are 0.10 less than the compression values (Table 8-4)
phi = 0.60 for all geomaterials where based on static uplift load tests; 0.80 for extreme event uplift
Shaft weight is a negative force effect in Eq. 10-1, not a resistance
equations: Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum[i=1..n](phi_S,i R_SN,i) — factored uplift resistance (side resistance only; numbered 10-32 in the print, p. 10-39)

sections.title: Design for Scour
sections.body: Scour reduces effective shaft length contributing to axial resistance. Design flood scour (Strength I): remove side and base resistance from scoured zone; check adequate resistance remains; also re-check lateral load resistance with reduced embedment. Scour check flood (Extreme Event II): more severe scour; check shaft tip depth provides adequate resistance. Three types of scour: general scour (entire channel cross-section), contraction scour (narrowing of flow area), local scour (around piers). Degradation scour (long-term channel bed lowering) must also be assessed. Side resistance above final scour elevation NOT counted. AASHTO: γEQ = 0.5 for Extreme Event II. Where scour controls, shaft must be extended deeper into the non-scoured stratum.
key_points: Scour: remove side and base resistance from scoured zone for all limit states
Design flood scour: Strength I; Check flood scour: Extreme Event II
Degradation scour (long-term) must be assessed in addition to design and check flood scour
Side resistance above final scour elevation not counted
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft design in stream environments subject to scour

sections.title: Downdrag
sections.body: Downdrag occurs when soil settles relative to shaft, reversing side resistance direction from upward (positive) to downward (negative). Common causes: consolidation of soft soils under fill or surcharge; liquefaction-induced ground settlement; drainage of soft soils. AASHTO: downdrag is a load effect (DD, factored by γDD = 1.25 for Strength I and IV); added to structural load demands. Shaft length must be sufficient that resistance below neutral plane (where side resistance reverses) equals sum of factored structural loads plus factored downdrag. Strategies to reduce downdrag: bituminous coating on shaft (reduces side adhesion in settling stratum); preloading or surcharging fill before construction; slender shafts in settling zone; use of pile isolation collar. Post-liquefaction downdrag: shaft settles with liquefied zone; combined kinematic + downdrag loading; compute using residual strength of liquefied soils.
key_points: Downdrag: soil settles relative to shaft; reverses side resistance to downward force
AASHTO: downdrag is load DD; γDD = 1.25 for Strength I and IV
Neutral plane: depth where cumulative side resistance equals structural + downdrag loads
Mitigation: bituminous coating; preloading; slender shafts in settling zone
Post-liquefaction downdrag: kinematic + downdrag; use residual strength of liquefied soils
sections.applicability: Drilled shafts in settling soils; fills over soft ground; post-liquefaction conditions

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter presented step-by-step LRFD procedure for design of drilled shafts under axial loading. Three geomaterial types (cohesionless, cohesive, rock) each with appropriate side and base resistance methods. Resistance factors depend on whether load testing is included in the project. Special considerations include scour, downdrag, and seismic effects on axial resistance. Design methods consistent with AASHTO LRFD 2017a.
